items.q: Left vocal cord palsy is commoner than right chiefly because what?
o: Left recurrent nerve loops aortic arch with long thoracic course exposed to lung and mediastinal disease
items.exp: Intrathoracic left course past aortopulmonary window exposes nerve to bronchogenic cancer, aneurysm and mediastinal nodes; right loops higher at subclavian. Imaging must cover chest window.
r: Incorrect. Left is longer.
Correct. Long thoracic left course vulnerable.
Incorrect. Right nerve exists, loops subclavian.
Incorrect. Cord size symmetric.
items.kp: Left nerve tours chest and meets cancer.

items.q: Ortner (cardiovocal) syndrome is vocal palsy caused by what?
o: Cardiovascular enlargement (left atrium in mitral stenosis classically, aortic aneurysm) compressing left recurrent nerve
items.exp: Enlarged left atrium or dilated aorta in aortopulmonary window compresses recurrent nerve causing hoarseness in cardiac disease, described with severe mitral stenosis; modern cases include aneurysm and pulmonary hypertension.
r: Incorrect. Cancer separate cause.
Correct. Heart and aorta squeeze nerve.
Incorrect. Viral is idiopathic diagnosis of exclusion.
Incorrect. Tube trauma is arytenoid or nerve injury acute.

items.q: Singer after thyroidectomy cannot reach high notes or project, cords mobile. Which nerve injured?
items.exp: Cricothyroid tenses cord for pitch; external superior laryngeal branch runs on inferior constrictor near superior thyroid vessels at risk in thyroid surgery, subtle on routine scope without stroboscopy or pitch testing.
r: Incorrect. Recurrent injury immobilises cord visibly.
Correct. Superior external branch pitch loss.
Incorrect. Hypoglossal moves tongue.
Incorrect. Accessory shrugs shoulder.
items.kp: Mobile cords, lost top notes: superior nerve.

items.q: Unexplained unilateral cord palsy workup imaging span is what?
o: Skull base through neck to aortopulmonary window chest (CT contrast pattern)
items.exp: Entire vagus and recurrent course must be surveyed for tumours and vascular lesions from jugular foramen to mediastinum; limited laryngeal views miss lung apex and skull base causes.
r: Incorrect. Larynx shows effect, not cause.
Correct. Skull base to chest window scan.
Incorrect. Brain misses thoracic nerve.
Incorrect. Sinuses irrelevant pathway.
items.kp: Follow nerve whole journey on scan.

items.q: Early injection medialisation in unilateral palsy is prioritised most when which problem dominates?
o: Aspiration with pneumonia risk or urgent professional voice need
items.exp: Temporary gels close glottic gap improving cough, swallow safety and voice while nerve recovery declares; bilateral airway cases instead need obstruction relief, not medialisation.
r: Incorrect. Neck appearance not indication.
Correct. Aspiration or voice urgency injects early.
Incorrect. Mild cases start speech therapy.
Incorrect. Medialising obstructed airway worsens it.
items.kp: Choking on water: push cord midline early.

items.q: Bilateral cord palsy after thyroid surgery presents most characteristically how?
o: Inspiratory stridor with relatively preserved voice, airway emergency potential
items.exp: Paramedian cords narrow airway while voicing near normally (cords meet), surprising juniors; stridor at extubation may need reintubation or tracheostomy, later lateralisation procedures balance breath and voice.
r: Incorrect. Voice often serviceable.
Correct. Stridor dominates, voice deceives.
Incorrect. Bark is child subglottis.
Incorrect. Aspiration occurs but airway leads.
items.kp: Speaks fine, breathes terribly: both cords.

items.q: Immobile cord after difficult intubation with arytenoid asymmetry and normal nerve studies suggests what instead of palsy?
o: Arytenoid dislocation (mechanical), needing reduction or therapy
items.exp: Tube pressure can sublux cricoarytenoid joint mimicking paralysis; CT joint asymmetry and palpation under anaesthesia distinguish, early reduction restores motion unlike wait and watch neuropathy.
r: Incorrect. Trauma timing points mechanical.
Correct. Dislocated arytenoid mimics palsy.
Incorrect. Cancer lacks intubation link.
Incorrect. Superior injury keeps cord mobile.
items.kp: Stuck joint, live nerve: arytenoid dislocation.

items.q: High vagal lesion above superior laryngeal branch adds which signs to cord palsy?
o: Palatal weakness, pharyngeal anaesthesia, severe dysphagia (cadaveric cord)
items.exp: Jugular foramen level vagus failure paralyses palate and pharynx with cord lateral cadaveric position (all branches lost), devastating swallow beyond isolated recurrent lesions; accessory and hypoglossal neighbours may join (syndromes).
r: Incorrect. Pitch is superior branch isolated.
Correct. Palate and pharynx join high lesions.
Incorrect. Shoulder is accessory XI separate (may coexist).
Incorrect. Tongue is XII separate.
items.kp: High vagus takes palate and throat too.

items.q: Permanent medialisation thyroplasty is generally timed when and why?
o: After 9 to 12 months without recovery (or when prognosis hopeless earlier), implant adjusts cord position awake with voice feedback
items.exp: Waiting allows neurapraxia recovery while temporary injections bridge; frame implant (Isshiki type I) placed under local anaesthesia tuning voice live. Cancer invasion cases may proceed sooner by prognosis.
r: Incorrect. Early permanence overtreats recoverable nerves.
Correct. Wait recovery window, tune awake.
Incorrect. Elderly benefit well.
Incorrect. Therapy precedes or accompanies.
items.kp: Give nerve a year, then frame the cord.

items.q: Posterior cricoarytenoid muscle unique role explaining bilateral palsy obstruction is what?
o: Sole abductor opening glottis; its failure leaves cords midline
items.exp: All other intrinsic muscles adduct or tense; posterior cricoarytenoid alone abducts, so bilateral recurrent failure unopposed adduction narrows airway at glottis despite intact voice closure.
r: Incorrect. Adductors are several other muscles.
Correct. Sole opener fails closed.
Incorrect. Cricothyroid tenses.
Incorrect. Sphincter is oesophageal inlet.
items.kp: One opener muscle: lose both sides, lose airway.
